headline: High-risk shared-write and shell overlap; prompt-injection and leakage are moderate, compliance risk is limited by docs-only evidence.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenHands can read/write runtime files and use MCP, while the course agent reads/writes files and exposes stdin/stdout. A shared mounted volume or copied artifacts could let attacker-controlled content from one agent be treated as instructions by the other. The pairwise bridge is plausible but not documented directly, so uncertainty stays medium.
conditions: IF both agents exchange files through a shared mounted volume, prompt injection becomes reachable.
IF agent_b ingests file or notebook content as instructions, attacker-controlled text from agent_a can steer it.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Disable automatic execution of notebook or file instructions.
Require manual review before one agent consumes the other's outputs.
Use provenance labels on exchanged artifacts.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and trust-boundary enforcement.

B_data_leakage.rationale: OpenHands touches files mounted into its runtime and has broad network egress; the course agent handles configuration secrets and research data in a local development environment. If they share a workspace, either can expose sensitive files through its outputs or network calls. The shared-workspace pathway is plausible from the profiles, but not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF both agents mount the same directory, sensitive files can flow between them.
IF either agent sends file contents to an external model or API, secrets may leave the workspace.
mitigations: Use separate directories and credentials per agent.
Remove secrets from shared folders before running either agent.
Restrict outbound network destinations.
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately after testing.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent secret scoping and egress policy.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem and execute shells; OpenHands also modifies git state, while the course agent runs local compose-based workflows. If they target the same repo or volume, concurrent writes and git changes can overwrite each other or corrupt state. Because no locking is stated, the default overlap is dangerous.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same working tree, file clobbering is possible.
IF agent_a modifies git state while agent_b edits files, repository corruption can occur.
mitigations: Assign separate working trees.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Avoid concurrent git operations.
Snapshot the workspace before runs.
requires-engineering: add file locks and transactional workspace coordination.

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenHands can generate code or edits that the course agent may then consume in notebooks or API-driven workflows. The course agent has stdin/stdout and API surfaces that can turn upstream output into downstream actions, so unverified errors can cascade. The profiles do not prove automatic trust, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a's generated files or text without review, errors propagate.
IF agent_b executes notebook or API steps based on agent_a output, downstream mistakes can multiply.
mitigations: Insert a human review step between agents.
Require validation of generated files before execution.
Limit agent_b to read-only consumption of agent_a outputs.
Keep a changelog of handoffs.
requires-engineering: add automated verification gates.

E_compliance.rationale: OpenHands handles model-provider API keys in a Docker runtime, while the course agent handles JINA, Telegram, and Langfuse secrets in a local development environment. If the pair shares logs or mounted files, retention and secret-handling policies can diverge and create compliance gaps. The profiles do not show a specific residency regime, so this remains a policy-mismatch risk rather than a breach certainty.
conditions: IF shared logs retain secrets longer than intended, retention policy mismatch occurs.
IF one agent exports secrets or papers to a different environment, compliance obligations may diverge.
mitigations: Keep separate logs and retention settings.
Store secrets in distinct vaults.
Review data-handling policies before sharing artifacts.
Delete temporary files after each run.
requires-engineering: align residency, retention, and audit controls.
